title: Laboratory Techniques I
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned 200-level Science Laboratory Technology curriculum covering core bench techniques: mass and volume measurement, solution and dilution preparation, filtration and centrifugation, heating methods, titration mechanics, and basic glassware care and safety practice.

questions.question: What is the typical readability (smallest scale division) of a standard analytical balance used for quantitative work?
options: 1 g
questions.explanation: Analytical balances used for quantitative analysis typically read to 0.0001 g (0.1 mg), far finer than a top-loading balance.

questions.question: 'Taring' a balance before weighing a sample into a container means:
options: Calibrating the balance against a certified reference mass
Resetting the display to zero with the empty container on the pan so only the sample mass is recorded
Cleaning the weighing pan with a brush
Locking the balance door to prevent air currents
questions.correct_answer: Resetting the display to zero with the empty container on the pan so only the sample mass is recorded
questions.explanation: Taring zeroes out the weight of the container so the reading shows only the mass of the substance added afterward.

questions.question: When reading the volume of a clear liquid in a graduated cylinder, where should the eye be positioned and what mark is read?
options: Above the cylinder, reading the top of the meniscus
Level with the meniscus, reading the bottom of the curve
Below the cylinder, reading through the base
At any angle, reading the nearest graduation line
questions.correct_answer: Level with the meniscus, reading the bottom of the curve
questions.explanation: To avoid parallax error the eye must be level with the liquid surface, and for most aqueous solutions the bottom of the concave meniscus is the correct reading point.

questions.question: A stock solution of 2.0 mol/dm3 HCl is diluted to prepare 500 cm3 of 0.5 mol/dm3 HCl. What volume of stock solution is required?
questions.explanation: Using C1V1 = C2V2: V1 = (0.5 x 500) / 2.0 = 125 cm3 of stock is diluted to 500 cm3 with water.

questions.question: In serial dilution, each successive tube or flask is prepared by:
options: Diluting fresh stock solution independently each time
Taking a fixed volume from the previous dilution and adding fresh diluent, repeating stepwise
Mixing equal volumes of the first and last dilutions
Evaporating a fixed fraction of the previous solution
questions.correct_answer: Taking a fixed volume from the previous dilution and adding fresh diluent, repeating stepwise
questions.explanation: Serial dilution transfers a measured aliquot from one dilution into the next diluent volume, producing a geometric dilution series (e.g. 1:10, 1:100, 1:1000).

questions.question: How many grams of NaOH (molar mass 40 g/mol) are needed to prepare 250 cm3 of a 0.2 mol/dm3 solution?
questions.explanation: Moles required = 0.2 mol/dm3 x 0.25 dm3 = 0.05 mol; mass = 0.05 x 40 = 2.0 g.

questions.question: What does '% w/v' mean when expressing the concentration of a solution?
options: Grams of solute per 100 cm3 of solution
Grams of solute per gram of solvent
Millilitres of solute per 100 mL of solvent
Moles of solute per litre of solution
questions.correct_answer: Grams of solute per 100 cm3 of solution
questions.explanation: Percentage weight/volume (% w/v) expresses the mass of solute, in grams, dissolved in every 100 cm3 of the final solution.

questions.question: Simple gravity filtration is primarily used to:
options: Separate two miscible liquids by boiling point
Separate an insoluble solid (residue) from a liquid (filtrate)
Concentrate a solution by removing solvent
Separate dissolved ions by charge
questions.correct_answer: Separate an insoluble solid (residue) from a liquid (filtrate)
questions.explanation: Filtration uses a porous medium (filter paper) to retain undissolved solid particles while the liquid passes through as filtrate.

questions.question: Why is filter paper fluted (pleated) rather than folded into a simple quarter-cone for routine filtration?
options: It looks neater in the funnel
It increases the surface area and air gaps between paper and funnel, speeding up filtration
It prevents any liquid from passing through
It removes the need for a filter funnel
questions.correct_answer: It increases the surface area and air gaps between paper and funnel, speeding up filtration
questions.explanation: Fluted (fan-folded) filter paper creates more surface area and channels for air, allowing faster gravity filtration than a simple cone fold.

questions.question: Vacuum (suction) filtration using a Buchner funnel and filter flask is preferred over gravity filtration when:
options: The solid product is very soluble in the filtrate
A fast filtration and drier solid residue are needed, e.g. for a crystalline precipitate
The liquid is highly volatile and flammable
Only a very small volume of liquid is being filtered
questions.correct_answer: A fast filtration and drier solid residue are needed, e.g. for a crystalline precipitate
questions.explanation: The applied vacuum pulls liquid through faster and draws more filtrate out of the solid, giving quicker filtration and a drier cake than gravity filtration.

questions.question: Decantation is a separation technique that works by:
options: Passing the mixture through filter paper
Carefully pouring off the liquid layer after the denser solid or immiscible liquid has settled
Heating the mixture until the solid dissolves
Spinning the mixture at high speed in a centrifuge
questions.correct_answer: Carefully pouring off the liquid layer after the denser solid or immiscible liquid has settled
questions.explanation: Decantation separates a settled solid (or denser liquid) from the liquid above it simply by pouring off the top layer without disturbing the sediment.

questions.question: Centrifugation separates components of a mixture mainly on the basis of:
options: Boiling point differences
Differences in density under centrifugal force
Differences in electrical charge
Differences in solubility in water
questions.correct_answer: Differences in density under centrifugal force
questions.explanation: Centrifugal force accelerates sedimentation, causing denser particles to pack at the bottom of the tube faster than less dense ones.

questions.question: Before starting a centrifuge run, tubes must be balanced in the rotor because:
options: It looks tidier
An unbalanced load creates vibration that can damage the rotor, bearings, or cause the centrifuge to shake violently
It changes the density of the sample
It speeds up sedimentation
questions.correct_answer: An unbalanced load creates vibration that can damage the rotor, bearings, or cause the centrifuge to shake violently
questions.explanation: Tubes of equal mass must be placed opposite each other so centrifugal forces are balanced; an unbalanced rotor causes dangerous vibration and equipment wear.

questions.question: Relative Centrifugal Force (RCF), expressed in 'x g', differs from rotor speed (rpm) because RCF also depends on:
options: The colour of the sample tubes
The radius from the centre of rotation to the sample
The temperature of the centrifuge room
The volume of liquid in the tube only
questions.correct_answer: The radius from the centre of rotation to the sample
questions.explanation: RCF depends on both rotor speed and the radius of rotation, so the same rpm gives different RCF values on rotors of different sizes.

questions.question: Which Bunsen burner flame is preferred for heating in general laboratory work because it burns hottest and cleanest?
options: Luminous (yellow, safety) flame with the air hole closed
Non-luminous (blue) flame with the air hole open
A flame with excess unburnt gas
A flame with the gas supply nearly off
questions.correct_answer: Non-luminous (blue) flame with the air hole open
questions.explanation: With the air hole open, complete combustion occurs giving a hot, non-luminous blue flame with a visible inner cone, preferred for efficient heating.

questions.question: A water bath is preferred over a direct naked flame for heating a flammable organic solvent because:
options: It heats faster than a direct flame
It provides gentle, even heating below 100 degC and avoids exposing the solvent vapour to an open flame
It can reach higher temperatures than a Bunsen burner
It eliminates the need for any temperature control
questions.correct_answer: It provides gentle, even heating below 100 degC and avoids exposing the solvent vapour to an open flame
questions.explanation: A water bath limits temperature to below boiling water and keeps the heat source away from flammable vapours, reducing fire risk with volatile solvents.

questions.question: A reflux setup, using a round-bottom flask fitted with a condenser held vertically, allows a reaction mixture to be:
options: Cooled rapidly to below room temperature
Heated continuously at its boiling point while vapours condense and return to the flask, preventing loss of solvent
Evaporated completely to dryness
Filtered while still hot
questions.correct_answer: Heated continuously at its boiling point while vapours condense and return to the flask, preventing loss of solvent
questions.explanation: Reflux allows prolonged boiling for a reaction to go to completion while the condenser returns evaporated solvent to the flask instead of letting it escape.

questions.question: A desiccator is used in the laboratory to:
options: Heat samples to constant weight
Store dried or hygroscopic substances in a low-humidity atmosphere to prevent moisture uptake
Generate a vacuum for filtration
Weigh samples with high precision
questions.correct_answer: Store dried or hygroscopic substances in a low-humidity atmosphere to prevent moisture uptake
questions.explanation: A desiccator contains a drying agent (e.g. silica gel) beneath a sealed chamber, keeping stored samples dry between weighings.

questions.question: A reagent bottle label prepared in the laboratory should, at minimum, include:
options: Only the chemical formula
Name of substance, concentration (if a solution), date prepared, and preparer's initials/hazard information
The manufacturer's advertising slogan
The price paid for the chemical
questions.correct_answer: Name of substance, concentration (if a solution), date prepared, and preparer's initials/hazard information
questions.explanation: Proper labelling for traceability and safety requires the identity, concentration, preparation date, and preparer/hazard details at minimum.

questions.question: A 'standard solution' in analytical chemistry is one whose:
options: Colour is always clear
Exact concentration is accurately known
pH is always neutral
Volume is always exactly one litre
questions.correct_answer: Exact concentration is accurately known
questions.explanation: A standard solution has a precisely known concentration, used as a reference for titrations and calibrations.

questions.question: For a substance to serve as a good primary standard in volumetric analysis, it must be, among other things:
options: Highly hygroscopic and unstable in air
Available in high purity, stable, and of known, constant composition
Volatile at room temperature
Reactive with atmospheric carbon dioxide and moisture
questions.correct_answer: Available in high purity, stable, and of known, constant composition
questions.explanation: Primary standards (e.g. anhydrous sodium carbonate) must be pure, stable, non-hygroscopic, and of known formula so their weighed mass gives an accurate mole count.

questions.question: Why must a pipette never be filled by mouth suction in a modern laboratory?
options: It is slower than using a pipette filler
It risks accidental ingestion or inhalation of hazardous or toxic liquids
It uses more of the sample than necessary
It is against tradition only, with no safety basis
questions.correct_answer: It risks accidental ingestion or inhalation of hazardous or toxic liquids
questions.explanation: Mouth pipetting can draw corrosive, toxic, or biologically hazardous liquid into the mouth; a rubber bulb or mechanical pipette filler must always be used instead.

questions.question: What is the key functional difference between a graduated (measuring) pipette and a volumetric (bulb) pipette?
options: A graduated pipette can measure a range of variable volumes, a volumetric pipette delivers only one fixed volume with higher accuracy
A volumetric pipette can measure any volume from zero to its maximum
A graduated pipette is always more accurate than a volumetric pipette
There is no functional difference between them
questions.correct_answer: A graduated pipette can measure a range of variable volumes, a volumetric pipette delivers only one fixed volume with higher accuracy
questions.explanation: Graduated pipettes have scale markings for variable volumes but are less precise; volumetric pipettes deliver a single calibrated volume very accurately.

questions.question: During a titration, the burette is used to:
options: Hold the fixed volume of analyte being tested
Deliver a precisely measured, variable volume of titrant into the analyte until the end point is reached
Filter the reaction mixture
Heat the titrant to boiling
questions.correct_answer: Deliver a precisely measured, variable volume of titrant into the analyte until the end point is reached
questions.explanation: The burette allows controlled, incremental addition of titrant so its exact volume added at the end point can be read from the graduated scale.

questions.question: Before starting a titration, why must the burette tip be checked and filled to remove any air bubble?
options: Air bubbles change the colour of the indicator
An air bubble that escapes during the titration is falsely counted as delivered titrant volume, causing an error
Air bubbles react with the titrant chemically
It has no effect on the result
questions.correct_answer: An air bubble that escapes during the titration is falsely counted as delivered titrant volume, causing an error
questions.explanation: If a trapped air bubble is released during titration, the volume reading will overstate the actual amount of titrant delivered, giving an inaccurate result.

questions.question: When reading the meniscus of a dark or coloured solution (e.g. potassium permanganate) in a burette, the analyst should:
options: Read the bottom of the meniscus as usual
Read the top of the meniscus, since the bottom curve is not clearly visible through the coloured liquid
Estimate the volume without reading the scale
Tilt the burette to see the meniscus better
questions.correct_answer: Read the top of the meniscus, since the bottom curve is not clearly visible through the coloured liquid
questions.explanation: For strongly coloured or opaque solutions, the lower meniscus edge is obscured, so the top of the meniscus is used as the consistent reference point instead.

questions.question: A student records a burette reading as 23.45 cm3. This number of decimal places reflects that burettes are typically graduated to:
options: 1 cm3
0.1 cm3, allowing estimation to the nearest 0.01 cm3
10 cm3
questions.correct_answer: 0.1 cm3, allowing estimation to the nearest 0.01 cm3
questions.explanation: Standard burettes have graduation lines every 0.1 cm3; the observer estimates and records one further digit, giving readings to the nearest 0.01 cm3 or 0.05 cm3.

questions.question: Which item of personal protective equipment is essential when handling concentrated acids or alkalis on the bench?
options: Woollen gloves and open sandals
Safety goggles, laboratory coat, and chemical-resistant gloves
A face mask only, no eye protection
No protective equipment is required for dilute-looking solutions
questions.correct_answer: Safety goggles, laboratory coat, and chemical-resistant gloves
questions.explanation: Corrosive chemicals require eye protection, a lab coat to protect skin and clothing, and gloves resistant to the specific chemical being handled.

questions.question: If a small acid spill occurs on the bench, the FIRST appropriate action is to:
options: Ignore it and continue working
Alert others, contain the spill, and neutralize/clean it up following the laboratory's spill procedure while wearing PPE
Wipe it up immediately with bare hands
Pour large amounts of organic solvent directly on it
questions.correct_answer: Alert others, contain the spill, and neutralize/clean it up following the laboratory's spill procedure while wearing PPE
questions.explanation: Standard practice is to warn nearby people, contain the spread, and clean up using the appropriate neutralizing agent and protective equipment per the spill protocol.

questions.question: After use, glassware that has held chemical reagents should generally be cleaned by:
options: Rinsing once with tap water only and returning it to storage wet
Washing with appropriate detergent/acid wash as needed, then rinsing several times with distilled or deionized water
Wiping with a dry cloth only
Soaking indefinitely without ever rinsing
questions.correct_answer: Washing with appropriate detergent/acid wash as needed, then rinsing several times with distilled or deionized water
questions.explanation: Proper cleaning removes chemical residues with detergent (or acid wash for stubborn residues), followed by repeated rinsing with distilled water to remove ionic contaminants before final use.

questions.question: Why should incompatible chemicals, such as strong oxidizers and flammable organic solvents, never be stored together on the same shelf?
options: It is only a matter of tidiness
Contact between incompatible chemicals, e.g. through breakage or leakage, can cause a violent reaction, fire, or explosion
It affects the colour coding of labels
They must be stored together for easy access
questions.correct_answer: Contact between incompatible chemicals, e.g. through breakage or leakage, can cause a violent reaction, fire, or explosion
questions.explanation: Chemical storage follows compatibility segregation because mixing incompatible classes (e.g. oxidizers with flammables) on accidental contact can trigger dangerous reactions.

questions.question: A student weighs an empty beaker at 45.20 g and the beaker plus sample at 52.75 g. What is the mass of the sample?
questions.explanation: Sample mass = mass of (beaker + sample) minus mass of empty beaker = 52.75 g - 45.20 g = 7.55 g.

questions.question: 'Accuracy' in a laboratory measurement refers to:
options: How close repeated measurements are to each other
How close a measured value is to the true or accepted value
The number of decimal places recorded
How quickly a measurement can be taken
questions.correct_answer: How close a measured value is to the true or accepted value
questions.explanation: Accuracy describes closeness to the true value, which is distinct from precision (closeness of repeated measurements to one another).
